questiontext.text:
For each statement, decide whether it is an identity (true for every angle \(x\) for which both sides are defined) or not an identity.

generalfeedback.text:
One value of \(x\) where the two sides differ is enough to show a statement is not an identity. Algebra with \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\) shows a statement is one.

  • \({@st1@}\): [[if test="is1"]]identity. [[else]]not an identity. [[/if]]{@tx1@}
  • \({@st2@}\): [[if test="is2"]]identity. [[else]]not an identity. [[/if]]{@tx2@}
  • \({@st3@}\): [[if test="is3"]]identity. [[else]]not an identity. [[/if]]{@tx3@}
  • \({@st4@}\): [[if test="is4"]]identity. [[else]]not an identity. [[/if]]{@tx4@}

questiondescription.text:
Trigonometry III: identity or not an identity

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.5: Decide which of four trigonometric statements are identities, using algebra or a counterexample.

Core

This question is original to this project.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: [[if test="is(nE = 1)"]]One of the statements you called an identity is not one.[[else]]{@nE@} of the statements you called identities are not.[[/if]] A statement can be true for several angles and still not be an identity. Test each of your identities at \(x = 0^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\): an identity holds at every angle where both sides are defined.

[[if test="is(nI = 1)"]]One of the statements you called not an identity is true for every angle.[[else]]{@nI@} of the statements you called not an identity are true for every angle.[[/if]] Before you reject a statement, find an angle where its two sides differ. If you cannot, look for algebra with \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\) or \(\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) that turns one side into the other.
